subject: ela
intro: These problems test how the parts of an argument work together. You will judge conclusions, evidence, reasons, transitions, organization, and formal style across multi-sentence paragraphs and short sources. Read each full stimulus before you answer.

items.prompt: Read this argument paragraph. 'Our middle school should add a recycling program. Each week the cafeteria throws away dozens of bottles and cans that could be recycled instead. A 2022 district report found that schools with recycling bins cut their landfill waste by nearly forty percent. Students could take turns managing the bins, which would teach responsibility.' Write a concluding statement that follows from this whole argument. Explain why your conclusion fits while a sentence about a new topic would not.
items.answer: A strong conclusion restates the claim and reflects the reasons. Example: 'For these reasons, a recycling program would reduce our school's waste and give students a meaningful responsibility, so the school should start one.' It must not introduce a new idea such as planting trees or buying new lunch trays.

steps: Identify the claim: the school should add a recycling program.
Identify the reasons given: it reduces wasted bottles and cans, the district report shows recycling cuts landfill waste, and it teaches students responsibility.
A conclusion must restate the claim and echo those reasons, not add a brand-new point.

Write a sentence that ties back to the claim and the reasons: 'For these reasons, a recycling program would reduce our school's waste and give students responsibility, so the school should start one.'
A sentence introducing a new topic, such as planting a garden, fails because it does not follow from the reasons already given.

items.prompt: Read the claim and the four possible reason-and-evidence pairings. Claim: 'The school library should stay open one hour after school.' Pairing A: 'because reading is fun, and lots of kids like books.' Pairing B: 'because many students lack a quiet place to study at home, and a 2021 survey found that thirty-eight percent of students share a bedroom.' Pairing C: 'because the library is a really big room.' Pairing D: 'because the librarian is very nice to everyone.' Which pairing gives the strongest reason backed by relevant evidence? Explain why it is stronger than the others.
items.answer: Pairing B is strongest. It states a logical reason (students lack a quiet study space) and backs it with a concrete, relevant statistic (38 percent share a bedroom). A relies on opinion with no evidence, C and D give facts that do not support keeping the library open.

steps: A reason must logically support the claim, and its evidence must be concrete and relevant.
Pairing B gives a reason (no quiet place at home) and pairs it with a survey statistic that directly supports that reason.
Pairing A offers an opinion ('reading is fun') with no factual evidence.
Pairing C and D state facts (the room is big, the librarian is nice) that do not explain why the library should stay open longer.
Because only B pairs a logical reason with relevant evidence, B is the strongest.

items.prompt: Read this argument paragraph, which contains one sentence that does not belong. 'Students should have a longer lunch period. A longer lunch would let students eat without rushing, which is better for digestion. It would also give them time to relax before afternoon classes. The cafeteria recently repainted its walls a bright shade of blue. With more time, students could finish their meals and return to class ready to focus.' Identify the sentence that should be removed and explain why it weakens the argument.
items.answer: Remove 'The cafeteria recently repainted its walls a bright shade of blue.' It is irrelevant because the wall color does not support the claim that lunch should be longer, even though it mentions the cafeteria.

steps: Identify the claim: students should have a longer lunch period.
Check each sentence against the claim. Eating without rushing, time to relax, and returning ready to focus all support a longer lunch.
The sentence about repainted blue walls mentions the cafeteria but says nothing about lunch length.
Because it does not support the claim, it is irrelevant and weakens the argument's focus.
Remove the wall-color sentence to keep every sentence tied to the claim.

items.prompt: Read these two short sources. Source 1: 'A 2020 study found that students who sleep at least nine hours score higher on tests than students who sleep less.' Source 2: 'Most middle schoolers naturally fall asleep later at night because of changes in their body clocks.' A student is arguing that the school day should start later. Using both sources, write one or two sentences that combine them into a logical argument, and explain how the two sources connect.
items.answer: Example: 'Because middle schoolers naturally fall asleep later (Source 2), an earlier start time prevents them from getting the nine hours that lead to higher test scores (Source 1). Therefore, a later start would help students sleep enough and perform better.' Source 2 explains why students struggle to sleep early, and Source 1 shows the benefit of more sleep, so together they support a later start.

steps: Identify the claim: the school day should start later.
Source 2 explains the cause: middle schoolers' body clocks make them fall asleep later.
Source 1 gives the benefit: more sleep leads to higher test scores.
Connect them: because students fall asleep late, an early start blocks the sleep that improves scores, so starting later helps.
Combine into a logical statement and use a cause-and-effect transition such as 'because' or 'therefore' to show the relationship.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph from a student argument that uses informal language. 'Look, school uniforms are honestly the worst and totally kill our style. Nobody wants to wear the same boring outfit every single day. We should just get rid of them, no cap.' Rewrite the paragraph to maintain a formal style suitable for an argument, keeping the same position. Then explain what you changed.
items.answer: Example revision: 'School uniforms limit students' ability to express their individuality. Many students find wearing the same outfit each day discouraging. For these reasons, the school should reconsider its uniform policy.' Changes: removed slang ('no cap,' 'the worst,' 'totally kill'), removed the casual opener 'Look,' and replaced emotional exaggeration with reasoned, formal wording.

steps: A formal argument avoids slang, contractions, casual openers, and emotional exaggeration.
Identify the informal parts: 'Look,' 'honestly the worst,' 'totally kill our style,' 'no cap.'
Replace exaggeration with measured claims, for example 'limit students' ability to express individuality.'
Keep the same position (oppose uniforms) but state it in neutral, formal language.
End with a formal recommendation rather than 'just get rid of them.'

items.prompt: Read this argument and the four possible concluding sentences. Argument: 'Our town should build a new bike path. A bike path would give riders a safe place away from traffic. It would also encourage more people to exercise outdoors.' Conclusion A: 'In short, a safe, exercise-friendly bike path is worth building for our town.' Conclusion B: 'The town should also build a new swimming pool.' Conclusion C: 'Bikes come in many colors and styles.' Conclusion D: 'Traffic is a problem in many cities around the world.' Which conclusion best follows from the argument, and why do the others fail?
items.answer: Conclusion A best follows. It restates the claim and reflects both reasons (safety from traffic and encouraging exercise). B introduces a new proposal, C states an unrelated detail, and D drifts to a broad topic that does not restate this argument.

steps: Identify the claim and reasons: build a bike path; it is safe from traffic and encourages exercise.
A good conclusion restates the claim and reflects the reasons.
Conclusion A names a 'safe, exercise-friendly bike path' and recommends building it, matching both reasons.
Conclusion B adds a new idea (a swimming pool), so it does not follow.
Conclusion C and D wander to unrelated or overly broad statements, so they fail to conclude this argument.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph. 'The school should offer a coding club. Coding teaches problem-solving skills that help in many subjects. ____ a club would let beginners learn from classmates who already know how to code.' Choose the transition that best fits the blank from these options: 'However,' 'In addition,' 'In contrast,' 'Nevertheless.' Then explain why the relationship between the two sentences calls for that transition.
items.answer: 'In addition' fits best. The second sentence adds another supporting reason (peer learning) to the first reason (problem-solving skills), so it signals addition, not contrast. 'However,' 'In contrast,' and 'Nevertheless' all signal contrast, which does not match.

steps: Read both sentences. The first gives a reason (coding teaches problem-solving). The second gives another reason (beginners learn from classmates).
Both sentences support the same claim, so the relationship is addition, not contrast.
'In addition' signals that another supporting point is being added.
'However,' 'In contrast,' and 'Nevertheless' all signal contrast or opposition, which does not fit two supporting reasons.
Choose 'In addition.'

items.prompt: Read this claim and the evidence offered for it. Claim: 'Our school should serve breakfast for free to all students.' Evidence offered: 'because hungry students cannot focus, and besides, the lunchroom is painted a cheerful yellow.' Explain why this evidence fails to fully support the claim, and write a stronger piece of evidence that would.
items.answer: Part of the evidence is fine ('hungry students cannot focus') but the rest ('the lunchroom is painted yellow') is irrelevant. A stronger version: 'because hungry students cannot focus, and a 2021 study found that students who eat breakfast score higher on morning tests.' This replaces the off-topic detail with a relevant fact.

steps: Check whether each part of the evidence supports the claim that free breakfast should be served.
'Hungry students cannot focus' is relevant because it connects food to learning.
'The lunchroom is painted a cheerful yellow' is off-topic; wall color does not support free breakfast.
To strengthen the evidence, replace the irrelevant detail with a relevant fact or statistic about breakfast and performance.
Result: 'hungry students cannot focus, and a study found students who eat breakfast score higher on morning tests.'

items.prompt: Read these three sentences from an argument that are out of order. (1) 'Therefore, the school should add more water fountains in the hallways.' (2) 'Students often arrive at class thirsty because the few fountains we have are crowded between periods.' (3) 'A 2022 building survey counted only two working fountains for over four hundred students.' Put the sentences in the most logical order for an argument and explain your reasoning.
items.answer: Logical order: 2, 3, 1. Sentence 2 states the reason (crowded fountains leave students thirsty), sentence 3 provides supporting evidence (only two fountains for 400 students), and sentence 1 is the concluding claim ('Therefore, add more fountains'). Reason, then evidence, then conclusion builds the argument clearly.

steps: An argument typically moves from a reason to its evidence to a concluding claim.
Sentence 2 gives the reason: crowded fountains leave students thirsty.
Sentence 3 supplies the evidence: only two working fountains for over four hundred students.
Sentence 1 begins with 'Therefore,' marking it as the conclusion that the school should add fountains.
So the order is 2, 3, 1: reason, evidence, conclusion.

items.prompt: Read this short argument and decide which single revision most improves it. Argument: 'Field trips should happen more often. They are super fun and everybody loves them. Also, a museum visit last year helped my class understand history way better than the textbook did.' Revision A: Add a sentence about the cost of buses. Revision B: Replace 'They are super fun and everybody loves them' with 'They give students hands-on experiences that deepen learning.' Revision C: Delete the sentence about the museum visit. Revision D: Add an exclamation point to the first sentence. Which revision most improves the argument, and why?
items.answer: Revision B most improves it. It replaces a vague, informal opinion ('super fun and everybody loves them') with a formal, reasoned statement that supports the claim. A adds an off-topic objection, C removes the strongest evidence, and D makes the tone less formal.

steps: Identify the weak part: 'They are super fun and everybody loves them' is informal and gives no real reason.
Revision B swaps it for a formal reason (hands-on experiences deepen learning), strengthening the argument.
Revision A introduces cost, which is an objection, not an improvement to the claim.
Revision C deletes the museum example, which is the strongest supporting evidence.
Revision D adds an exclamation point, making the style less formal, so B is best.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph that mixes a claim, a reason, and evidence. 'The school should plant a vegetable garden. A garden would give students a chance to grow their own healthy food. A 2021 school survey found that sixty-five percent of students said they rarely eat fresh vegetables. Gardening is also a relaxing hobby for many adults.' Label each sentence as the claim, the reason, the supporting evidence, or an irrelevant detail. Explain your labels.
items.answer: Sentence 1 ('The school should plant a vegetable garden') is the claim. Sentence 2 ('A garden would give students a chance to grow healthy food') is the reason. Sentence 3 (the 65 percent survey statistic) is the supporting evidence. Sentence 4 ('Gardening is a relaxing hobby for many adults') is an irrelevant detail because it is about adults, not the student garden claim.

steps: The claim is the debatable position: 'The school should plant a vegetable garden.'
The reason explains why: 'A garden would give students a chance to grow healthy food.'
The evidence is the concrete fact that backs the reason: the 65 percent survey statistic about rarely eating vegetables.
The last sentence about adults' relaxing hobby does not support the claim about a student garden, so it is irrelevant.
Label: claim, reason, evidence, irrelevant detail.

items.prompt: Read this argument paragraph and the four concluding statements. Argument: 'The school should allow students to choose their own seats in class. Students concentrate better when they sit near friends they trust. A 2022 classroom study found that students in chosen seats finished assignments ten percent faster.' Conclusion A: 'In conclusion, letting students choose their seats helps them concentrate and work faster, so the school should allow it.' Conclusion B: 'Desks should be cleaned more often.' Conclusion C: 'Some students prefer sitting by the window.' Conclusion D: 'Friendship is one of the most important things in life.' Which conclusion best follows, and why are the others unfit?
items.answer: Conclusion A best follows. It restates the claim (allow chosen seats) and reflects both reasons (better concentration and faster work). B introduces cleaning, an unrelated idea. C adds a minor detail not in the argument. D drifts into a broad statement about friendship.

steps: Identify the claim and reasons: allow chosen seats; students concentrate better and finish work faster.
A good conclusion restates the claim and reflects both reasons.
Conclusion A names concentration and faster work and recommends allowing chosen seats, matching the argument.
Conclusion B (clean desks) introduces a new, unrelated idea.
Conclusion C names a minor detail and D makes a broad claim about friendship, so neither concludes this argument.

items.prompt: Read this argument that overstates its case. 'Banning gum in school is the worst rule ever invented, and any teacher who supports it clearly does not care about students at all.' Explain two problems with this sentence as an argument, then rewrite it to make a reasoned, formal claim against the gum ban.
items.answer: Two problems: it uses emotional exaggeration ('the worst rule ever invented') instead of reasoned support, and it attacks teachers personally ('does not care about students') instead of addressing the issue. Formal rewrite: 'The gum ban may be unnecessary, since chewing gum can help some students stay focused without disrupting class.'

steps: A strong argument uses reasoned, formal language and addresses the issue, not personal attacks.
Problem one: 'the worst rule ever invented' is emotional exaggeration, not evidence.
Problem two: 'any teacher who supports it does not care about students' attacks people instead of reasoning about the rule.
Rewrite with a measured claim and a reason: gum can help focus without disrupting class.
The result states a position formally and gives a reason rather than insulting anyone.

items.prompt: Read these two sentences that need a transition between them. 'Many students say homework helps them review what they learned. ____ a 2021 survey found that students who skipped homework scored lower on unit tests.' From the options 'However,' 'For example,' 'In contrast,' and 'Although,' choose the transition that best clarifies the relationship, and explain the logic.
items.answer: 'For example' fits best. The second sentence gives a specific instance of evidence that supports the first sentence's point that homework helps. 'However,' 'In contrast,' and 'Although' all signal contrast, but the survey agrees with the first sentence rather than opposing it.

steps: Read both sentences. The first claims homework helps review. The second gives a survey showing skipping homework lowers scores.
The survey supports the first sentence, so the relationship is illustration, not contrast.
'For example' introduces a specific instance that backs up the prior statement.
'However,' 'In contrast,' and 'Although' signal opposition, which does not match supporting evidence.
Choose 'For example.'

items.prompt: Read this full short argument, which has one weak spot. 'The school should extend recess to thirty minutes. Longer recess gives students more time to move, and exercise improves focus in class. A 2020 study found that students who exercised daily had better attention spans. Recess is also when I get to see my best friend Maya.' Identify the weakest sentence, explain why it weakens this argument, and suggest a replacement that would strengthen the argument.
items.answer: The weakest sentence is 'Recess is also when I get to see my best friend Maya.' It is a personal, informal detail that does not support the claim that recess should be longer. A stronger replacement: 'In addition, longer recess gives students time to settle disagreements through play, which reduces conflicts in class.'

steps: Identify the claim: extend recess to thirty minutes.
Check each sentence. Time to move, exercise improving focus, and the study on attention spans all support the claim.
'Recess is when I get to see my best friend Maya' is a personal, informal detail that does not support the claim.
Replace it with a formal reason-and-benefit statement that supports longer recess.
Example replacement: longer recess lets students settle disagreements through play, reducing classroom conflict.
